description: Reasoning under uncertainty: conditional probability and Bayes, random variables and their distributions, counting, random processes, and the statistics that turn data into evidence, with the ways it goes wrong. The `probability`, `randomness`, and `statistics` concepts live in mathematics.json.

concepts.title: Conditional Probability
concepts.summary: The probability of something once you know something else has happened. Learning that a card is red changes the chance it is a heart. Most sensible reasoning about evidence is conditional probability, and most mistakes come from confusing P(A given B) with P(B given A).

concepts.title: Bayes' Theorem
concepts.summary: How to update a belief when new evidence arrives: the new probability is proportional to the old one times how well the belief predicted the evidence. It explains why a positive result from an accurate test can still mean you are probably fine.

concepts.title: Independence
concepts.summary: Two events are independent when knowing one tells you nothing about the other: coin flips, dice rolls. Independence lets probabilities multiply. Much of statistics assumes it, and many failures, from financial crashes to bad polls, come from assuming it wrongly.

concepts.title: Bayesian Inference
concepts.summary: Treat probability as degree of belief and update it with data using Bayes' theorem. It gives a direct answer to how likely is this hypothesis given what I saw? and handles small data well, at the cost of having to state a prior.

concepts.title: Random Variables
concepts.summary: A number whose value depends on chance: the roll of a die, tomorrow's temperature, the time until the next bus. Giving chance a numeric form lets you talk about averages, spread, and the shape of all the possible outcomes.

concepts.title: Expected Value
concepts.summary: The average outcome you would get if you repeated a chance process forever, each result weighted by its probability. It is how insurers price risk and how gamblers can see that a lottery ticket costs more than it returns.

concepts.title: Variance
concepts.summary: How spread out a random quantity is around its average: the mean of the squared distance from the mean. Two investments can have the same expected return and very different variance, which is another word for risk.

concepts.title: Distributions
concepts.summary: The full description of a random quantity: how likely each value or range of values is. Different processes produce recognizable shapes, such as the bell curve, the counts of rare events, and the waiting times between them.

concepts.title: The Normal Curve
concepts.summary: The bell curve: symmetric around the mean, with most values close by and few far away. It appears when many small independent effects add up, which is why heights, measurement errors, and averages are all roughly normal.

concepts.title: Binomial Distribution
concepts.summary: The number of successes in a fixed number of independent tries, each with the same chance: heads in twenty flips, defective items in a batch, converts among visitors. It is the basic model behind polls and A/B tests.

concepts.title: Poisson Distribution
concepts.summary: The number of times a rare event happens in a fixed stretch of time or space when occurrences are independent: emails per hour, typos per page, radioactive decays per second. Its mean and variance are equal.

concepts.title: Exponential Distribution
concepts.summary: The waiting time until the next random event, when events happen at a constant average rate: the next customer, the next decay, the next failure. It has no memory: having waited an hour makes the wait no shorter.

concepts.title: Power Laws
concepts.summary: Distributions where a few cases are enormous and most are tiny: city sizes, wealth, word frequencies, earthquake energies. They have heavy tails, so the average can be dominated by rare extremes and the normal curve gives the wrong picture.

concepts.title: Uniform Distribution
concepts.summary: Every value in a range equally likely: a fair die, a random number generator. It is the starting point of simulation, since other distributions can be produced from uniform random numbers by transforming them.

concepts.title: Law of Large Numbers
concepts.summary: Averages settle down. As you collect more independent observations, their mean gets closer to the true expected value. It is why casinos win reliably over thousands of bets, and why a small sample can mislead.

concepts.title: Central Limit Theorem
concepts.summary: Add up many independent random effects, and the total looks like a bell curve, whatever shape each effect had. It is why the normal distribution is everywhere, and why averages are far more predictable than the individual values behind them.

concepts.title: Combinatorics
concepts.summary: The art of counting without listing: how many ways to arrange, choose, or split things. It is the foundation of probability, which is often counted possibilities, and of algorithm analysis, where the count of cases sets the cost.

concepts.title: Permutations
concepts.summary: The ways to put things in order. Three books can be lined up 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways, and twenty in more ways than there are seconds since the Earth formed. Permutations count orderings, where combinations count selections.

concepts.title: Combinations
concepts.summary: The ways to choose some things from a larger set when order does not matter: a poker hand, a committee, a lottery ticket. The count is n! / (k!(n − k)!), the entries of Pascal's triangle.

concepts.title: Factorials
concepts.summary: n! is the product of the whole numbers from 1 to n, the number of ways to order n things. It grows explosively: 10! is 3.6 million, 20! is about 2.4 × 10¹⁸. Its speed of growth is why brute force fails on ordering problems.

concepts.title: Pigeonhole Principle
concepts.summary: If you put more pigeons than holes, some hole has two. Simple as it sounds, it proves surprising things: two people in a big city have the same number of hairs, and any large enough set of numbers contains patterns.

concepts.title: Birthday Paradox
concepts.summary: In a room of 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is over half. It seems too small because we think about matches with ourselves, not among all pairs. The same math explains why hash collisions arrive so soon.

concepts.title: Inclusion–Exclusion
concepts.summary: To count things in overlapping groups, add the group sizes, subtract the overlaps you counted twice, add back the triple overlaps you removed too often, and so on. It turns messy overlaps into an exact formula.

concepts.title: Markov Chains
concepts.summary: A process that hops between states, where the next state depends only on the current one, not on how it arrived. It models weather, web surfing, board games, and text, and its long-run behavior settles into a stable pattern.

concepts.title: Random Walks
concepts.summary: A path made of random steps: a drunkard's stumbling, a gambler's fortune, a jiggling particle. After n steps the typical distance from the start grows only as the square root of n, which is why diffusion is slow but relentless.

concepts.title: MCMC
concepts.summary: A way of sampling from complicated distributions by building a Markov chain that wanders through the possibilities and spends time in proportion to their probability. It made much of modern Bayesian statistics practical.

concepts.title: Hidden Markov Models
concepts.summary: A Markov chain you cannot observe directly: you see only clues it emits. It decodes speech from sound, genes from DNA, and parts of speech from words, by working out the most likely hidden story behind the clues.

concepts.title: Brownian Motion
concepts.summary: The endless jitter of tiny particles in a fluid, caused by molecules bumping them. Einstein's 1905 analysis of it gave the first convincing evidence that atoms exist, and its mathematics underlies models of heat, diffusion, and stock prices.

concepts.title: Descriptive Statistics
concepts.summary: Summarizing a pile of data in a few numbers and pictures: where it is centered, how spread out it is, what shape it has. Description comes before inference, and a good summary can reveal what an average hides.

concepts.title: Averages
concepts.summary: Three ways to say what is typical. The mean adds and divides, the median is the middle value, the mode is the most common. They tell different stories when data is skewed: the average income can be far above what most people earn.

concepts.title: Standard Deviation
concepts.summary: The typical distance of values from their mean, in the same units as the data. About two thirds of a bell curve lies within one standard deviation, and 95 percent within two, which makes it the standard ruler for spread.

concepts.title: Percentiles
concepts.summary: The value below which a given share of the data falls. The median is the 50th percentile. Percentiles compare a person to a population, from exam scores to growth charts, and expose the tail that averages hide.

concepts.title: Outliers
concepts.summary: Points far from the rest. They may be errors, rare real events, or a sign that the assumed model is wrong. Deleting them silently can hide the most interesting thing in the data, and keeping them can distort every average.

concepts.title: Sampling
concepts.summary: Learning about a whole population by examining part of it. How the sample is chosen matters more than how big it is: a huge biased sample can be worse than a small random one.

concepts.title: Selection Bias
concepts.summary: When the way you gathered data makes some cases likelier to be included than others, so the sample misrepresents the population. Phone polls that miss people without phones, and surveys answered mostly by the motivated, are classic cases.

concepts.title: Margin of Error
concepts.summary: How far a survey result might be from the truth because of random sampling alone. A poll of a thousand people has a margin of about three percentage points. It says nothing about bias, wording, or who did not respond.

concepts.title: Correlation
concepts.summary: A measure of how closely two quantities move together, from −1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to +1 (in step). It finds patterns worth investigating, but on its own cannot say that one thing causes the other.

concepts.title: Regression
concepts.summary: Fitting a relationship between variables to predict one from the others, and to measure how strong each influence is. From forecasting sales to estimating drug effects, regression is the workhorse of applied statistics.

concepts.title: Linear Regression
concepts.summary: Fit the straight line, or plane, that comes closest to the data, and read off its slope as the effect of one variable on another. Simple, interpretable, and often good enough; it can be badly misleading when the relationship is not a line.

concepts.title: Least Squares
concepts.summary: Choose the fit that makes the sum of squared errors as small as possible. Gauss and Legendre introduced it around 1800 to combine astronomical measurements, and it remains the default way of fitting a model to noisy data.

concepts.title: Overfitting
concepts.summary: A model that has learned the noise as well as the pattern: it fits the data it was trained on beautifully and predicts new data badly. The remedy is to test on data the model has not seen, and to keep the model simple enough.

concepts.title: Hypothesis Testing
concepts.summary: A procedure for asking whether data is surprising if nothing is going on. Assume the boring explanation, the null hypothesis, and see how unlikely results as extreme as yours would be. If very unlikely, doubt the boring explanation.

concepts.title: P-Values
concepts.summary: The probability of seeing data at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true, the mistake most people make. Small values signal surprise, not importance.

concepts.title: Confidence Intervals
concepts.summary: A range of plausible values for a quantity, built so that in the long run 95 percent of such intervals would contain the truth. It says more than a single estimate, since it shows how uncertain the estimate is.

concepts.title: False Positives
concepts.wiki: Type I and type II errors
concepts.summary: Two ways a test can be wrong: a false alarm, seeing an effect that is not there (type I), and a miss, failing to see one that is (type II). Reducing one usually raises the other, so the balance depends on the cost of each mistake.

concepts.title: Multiple Comparisons
concepts.summary: Test enough things and some will look significant by chance: at the 5 percent level, one in twenty will. Studies that run dozens of comparisons and report the hits mislead, unless corrected for the number of tests.

concepts.title: P-Hacking
concepts.summary: Analyzing data in many ways until something reaches significance, then reporting only that. Each choice, dropping outliers, adding a covariate, choosing a subgroup, is defensible, but together they make false findings look real.

concepts.title: Replication Crisis
concepts.summary: The discovery, in the 2010s, that many published findings in psychology, medicine, and other fields fail to reproduce. Small samples, flexible analysis, and publication of only positive results made false discoveries common.

concepts.title: Experimental Design
concepts.summary: Planning a study so that it can answer the question: which comparisons to make, how many subjects, how to assign them, what to measure. A good design can settle cause; no analysis can rescue a bad one.

concepts.title: Controlled Trials
concepts.summary: Assign people at random to a treatment or a comparison group, so the groups differ only by chance and the treatment. Randomization is the most reliable way to show that something causes an effect, and the gold standard of medicine.

concepts.title: Confounding
concepts.summary: When a third factor influences both the supposed cause and the effect, creating a link that is not causal. Coffee drinkers may get more lung cancer because they smoke more. Confounders are why observation alone is treacherous.

concepts.title: Causal Inference
concepts.summary: Methods for working out what causes what, not just what goes with what: randomized trials, natural experiments, and causal diagrams. It asks the counterfactual question: what would have happened if things had been different?

concepts.title: Simpson's Paradox
concepts.summary: A trend that appears in every subgroup can reverse when the groups are combined. A treatment can look worse overall yet be better for every kind of patient, because the mix of patients differs. It shows why lumping data together can lie.

concepts.title: Regression to the Mean
concepts.summary: Extreme results tend to be followed by less extreme ones, purely by chance. The worst-performing schools improve and the best decline without anyone doing anything. Mistaking it for the effect of an intervention is a classic error.

concepts.title: Estimation
concepts.summary: Inferring the value of an unknown quantity from noisy data. Estimators are judged by bias, variance, and efficiency, and by how well they cope with small samples and outliers.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood
concepts.summary: Pick the parameter values that make the observed data most probable. It is the most widely used general method of estimation, behind logistic regression and most fitted models, and a bridge to Bayesian ideas.

concepts.title: The Bootstrap
concepts.summary: Estimate uncertainty by resampling your own data, with replacement, thousands of times, and seeing how the answer varies. It needs little theory and works for statistics that have no formula for their error.
